10.headline: Jack passes the hundredth arch as Bolek sleeps in the grass
10.issueTitle: The Hundredth Arch on the Queen's Lawn
10.deck: A milestone four weeks in the moving finally stands still, and the Queen takes a head for twenty-nine points nobody bothered to wake
10.column:
The Queen's croquet ground runs from the hedge to the horizon and nothing on it is what it was made to be.

The mallets are flamingos and they have views. The balls are hedgehogs and they uncurl mid-stroke and wander off to look at something. The arches are card soldiers bent double, and they stand where they like, and they walk when they feel like walking.

One thing only is counted here. Every arch a man passes in his life goes against his name, and there is no other honour on the lawn.

Jack came onto the grass on ninety-nine.

He had been coming onto it on ninety-nine for a month. Four times he had lined up the hundredth soldier, and four times the soldier had straightened, saluted, and strolled twenty paces to the left before the hedgehog reached him.

This time the soldier stood.

Jack struck 148.22 and went through clean, and the card did not move an inch, and somewhere behind the hedge a clock that had been stopped all autumn was heard to start.

One hundred career wins. Fifteen seasons of walking this lawn.

The man he took it from was Bolek, who is 2-8 and who leads Jack 6-5 across their lives, which means the arch that had refused nine other opponents was finally handed over by the one player in FantasyWorld Jack has never mastered.

Bolek played 119.64 and was not disgraced by it.

He had, however, left his best hedgehogs asleep in the long grass behind the tee. Twenty-nine and a half points of them, curled up warm, more than any man abandoned anywhere on the ground this week.

The Queen does not behead the loser. She beheads the man who loses worst while holding better.

29.58.

Off with his head. The belt is Bolek's, and Mario surrendered it to him without argument.

At the top of the lawn, Nate did something almost nobody does out here.

He used everything he owned.

Every hedgehog he had brought went through an arch. Not one dozing at the boundary, not one sniffing at the roses, not a single point left on the grass behind him. 157.08, and the basket empty.

Sixty-five times in one thousand and ten attempts has a man come off this ground with nothing left behind.

Daniel, opposite him, was guilty of one-tenth of a point of carelessness. He put up 122.58 and was beaten by 34.5, and there is no appeal available to a man whose only fault was a decimal.

Two soldiers now stand between Nate and the same hundred Jack has just passed. Ninety-eight. He has watched the arches walk away from other men all season, and he will now find out whether they walk away from him.

On the far side of the ground, something grew.

Jonathan Taylor is worth 25.14 on an ordinary afternoon. He got at whatever it is one gets at in that garden and came up 55.6, filling the lawn, knocking the hoops flat, and Mario simply walked behind him collecting arches.

165.3. Highest on the ground. Nine out of nine against every man in the league, which is the plain statement that no opponent existed who could have taken this off him.

Opposite that was Justin, who arrived holding first place in FantasyWorld.

Justin ran. He ran the way you have to run in that country, hard, arms going, and when he stopped he had 86.44 and was three places further back than when he started. Fourth. Beaten by 78.86. Nought for nine against the field, which is the exact opposite of the man across the lawn from him.

The lowest score of the week, from the man who spent this season being told his lineups were the tidiest in the league.

Bill was given two hedgehogs and told to choose.

He has been here before. Last time he chose the safe one and the animal he left in the basket had 23.1 in it, and he has heard about it since.

So he reached in and took RJ Harvey.

Harvey rolled one and a half feet and stopped.

1.8.

Kimani Vidal, left in the basket, was worth 20.8. A nineteen point difference between the hand Bill put in and the hand he did not. His flamingo then tucked its head under its wing and refused to look at the ball at all — 6.8 from Bo Nix, a bird that averages 20.64 and has never before declined to work.

Bill finished on 101.44, beaten by 38.9, and beaten also by eight of the nine other men on the lawn.

The man who beat him was Bryan, and here the ground finally cracked a joke worth hearing.

All season Bryan has played immaculately. Two perfect rounds, the best efficiency in FantasyWorld, nothing wasted, and defeat after defeat after defeat.

This week he left 20.46 lying in the grass.

He won by 38.9.

Eric/Blakey took 137.88 past Gabes, a second win running, and remain ninth on 3-7 — they have now beaten the leading scorer and beaten a six-win team inside a fortnight and it has moved them precisely nowhere. Gabes managed 107.12 and lost to seven of the nine men out there, having beaten Jack by forty a fortnight ago. The lawn is not consistent about anybody.

At dusk the card soldiers straighten up one by one and walk off to wherever they sleep, so that in the morning no arch is where a man left it.

Jack's hundredth stood still for exactly one stroke.

Nate has two of them to catch, and they are already moving.

priorColumns:
The burial ground at Hollow End is opened one night a year, and the men of FantasyWorld open it themselves, with spades, with hooded lanterns, without speaking.

There are two rules at the gate.

You are weighed on what you carry out. Whatever stays in the ground stays in the ground, and by first light the holes have closed again from underneath.

Ten men went over the wall.

Gabes went in first, because Gabes has been the best of them at this all season.

He put his spade into the softest plot in the yard and James Cook came up out of it.

On an ordinary night Cook is worth 15.87. He came up out of Hollow End with 41.6 in him, and he came up alone.

Gabes worked the rest of the row and the rest of the row was thin. Bone dust. Split boxes. Things not worth the lifting.

He reached the gate at grey light with 95.26 across his shoulders and the sexton did not trouble with the scale, because there was not one man in the county who had not out-carried him.

Nought for nine.

The lightest load in FantasyWorld, taken out of the ground by the team that went in ranked ahead of everybody.

He had also left 20.52 down there. That is the third week running he has uncovered something with his own hands and walked away from it, and by the time he looked back the earth was already moving.

At the far wall, alone, digging badly, was Bolek.

Bolek is the worst of them at this and has been since the season opened: fourteen nights ahead of the field, fifty-eight behind.

He found 104.08 at Hollow End. That is nothing. That is a bad night in a bad year.

He carried out 104.08.

All of it. Not a rag, not a knuckle, not a coin left under the clay — one empty hole and one man walking down to the gate with everything the ground had offered him strapped to his back. Sixty-five times in 1010 nights has anybody come out of that yard clean.

The sexton weighed them both.

8.82.

Three years ago Gabes met this same man on this same night and out-carried him by 82.9.

He went into Hollow End first in FantasyWorld and came out of it fourth.

Bill had two lids in front of him and one crowbar.

Under the first was Rico Dowdle, who had come up out of the ground three times this autumn averaging 28.97, and who was, on all the evidence available at the graveside, the safest body in the yard.

Bill went to Dowdle. He got him open and found 6.4 in him.

The second lid he never touched. RJ Harvey was lying under it with 23.1.

Bill left 26.84 at Hollow End, more than any man in the league, and the ground had taken it before he was over the wall. At the gate the sexton had the belt waiting for him. Bolek unbuckled it and handed it across, having for once nothing whatsoever to answer for.

Nate opened only what he meant to open.

He carried 143.96 out of that yard and left an empty hole behind him, and he beat Bill by 28.56. Last time out every single man in the county dug more than Nate did. This time he went 6-3 against the field and stood at the gate with clean hands.

Set into the church wall at Hollow End there is a stone the sexton cuts, and two men in this league are one name short of a hundred.

Daniel came in needing it.

Bryan met him in the dark.

For four weeks Bryan has been the man the others carried out of this yard — the tidiest work in FantasyWorld, and a hole waiting for him at the end of every night. He climbed out of this one himself. 149.52, and 4.28 left behind, which is near enough to nothing.

Daniel went back down the road with ninety-nine still against his name. Bryan is 2-6 against him lifetime, and it took a hundredth win to make one of those two matter.

Jack came in needing it as well.

Mario was waiting at the top of the yard with 158.16 on his back, the heaviest load anyone took out of Hollow End this year, and 9-0 against the field, which is the plain statement that there was no man in the county he would have lost to.

Jack left 23.3 in the ground and went home on ninety-nine.

Two men. One number. The stone unchanged.

Justin took the second-heaviest load of the night, 152.02, left the yard almost bare and holds first place in FantasyWorld on 6-2. Eric/Blakey were beaten by 39.08 and are 1-7, and their only comfort is that they have taken more out of this season than Bolek has and will not be thanked for it.

By first light every hole in the yard had closed. Not been filled. Closed.

Bill's 26.84 was gone. So was the twenty Gabes had stood over and decided against, and whatever Jack had thought he could come back for.

The ground at Hollow End keeps what you leave in it.

It has never once cared who found it first.

The Cassiopeia Club is cut into the top of a mountain and there is one way up to it, a cable car that leaves the valley station when the man in the booth decides it should.

Ten men in dinner jackets came up this week.

The house rule is printed nowhere and everybody knows it. The Cassiopeia does not pay the best hand in the room. It pays the man whose opponent did worse. You may lay down the finest cards of your life on that baize and go back down the mountain with your pockets turned out, provided you have been seated across from the right person.

Anselm Vare does not gamble. Vare does the placards.

Before the car arrives he walks the five tables with a leather folder under his arm, setting the little printed names down on the cloth, and then he stands at the window with a drink he never finishes and watches the weather come over the ridge. That is the entire scheme. Nobody has worked out how to beat it because there is nothing to beat. He decides who is opposite whom, and the mountain does the rest.

On the gallery above the floor there is a private room with a brass hundred screwed to the door.

Daniel had been standing outside it for three weeks.

Twice he had gone to the table needing one win and twice he had come back up the stairs and found the handle would not turn. This time Vare seated him across from Bolek, and dealt him a man nobody in the room had ever looked at twice.

Brock Bowers has been worth 3.94 a night all season. He fetches drinks. He stands behind chairs.

He sat down and put 35.3 on the cloth.

Bolek did not fold. He went to 119.28, which for Bolek is a genuine night's work, the best hand he has laid down in weeks, and it was short.

3.48.

The door on the gallery opened. Daniel went through it with one hundred career wins behind him, which is fifteen seasons of climbing this mountain, and the room did not stop for him because the room never stops for anybody.

Jack had come up the cable car on ninety-nine as well.

Vare had put him opposite Gabes, and Gabes arrived with his coat empty.

That is worth saying plainly. For three straight weeks Gabes has left money in his pockets — a man asleep in a bunkhouse, twenty points behind a locked door, a good hand held back for no reason anybody could name. This week he put down 148.54 and kept 1.5. Nothing hidden, nothing saved, nothing to answer for.

Jack managed 108.44. Eight of the nine other men in the room beat it. He went back down in the cable car with ninety-nine still against his name and two losses on the trot, and the brass door stayed shut.

Nate is on ninety-seven and climbing, three short, and he got there by doing something the house has always been happy to arrange.

He was seated across from Bryan.

Bryan played a flawless hand. Every card he was holding, he played. When the dealer cleared the table there was nothing left in his fingers — not one point on the bench, the second time in a handful of weeks he has emptied his hand completely, and it is the rarest thing anyone does at the Cassiopeia.

101.06.

The worst hand in the room. Every man on that mountain beat it. Nine out of nine, and the one sitting opposite him was Nate, who has now taken seven of the eight nights the two of them have ever spent at the same table.

Beaten by 42.04. Third in the league for efficiency all year, first actually, and 3-6, and back down the mountain in the dark.

Bill had the biggest stack of the night.

165.12, and there was not a man in the Cassiopeia he would have lost to. Vare sat him opposite Justin, who came up here holding first place, and Bill took 35.06 off him without hurrying.

And Justin walked out still top of the table, 6-3, because three men now hold that record and he has taken more off this season than either of them.

The house pays who the house pays.

Which brings us to the man who has taken more money out of this season than anybody alive and cannot get down the mountain with it.

Mario has 1294.44 for the year. Nobody is close. He sat down against Eric/Blakey, who have won twice in nine attempts, and he left 25.7 in his coat pocket — Alec Pierce with 16 in him, folded in the lining, in favour of Deebo Samuel and 4.9 on the cloth.

Eric/Blakey put down 161.18 and took the night by 15.3. Eight of the nine men in the room would have lost to them, which is the first time all season the seating plan has done them a kindness rather than an injury.

Mario is 5-4. At the cloakroom they handed him the belt.

By the time the last car went down, the gallery door had closed again with Daniel inside it, and the floor was being swept, and Vare was at the window with the folder open on the sill, laying out next week's placards in the dark.

He never looks at anyone's cards.

He only needs to know who is sitting opposite them.

11.headline: Bill abandons 47.1 on the far bank and is decorated anyway
11.issueTitle: What the Clerk Writes Down at Dawn
11.deck: A night of exchanges at the Gerberstrasse bridge, where the ledger records only which side of the white line a man was standing on.
11.column:
The bridge at Gerberstrasse is lit at both ends and dark in the middle. That is not an oversight. Two lamps, two barriers, and forty paces of nothing between them where a man cannot be seen from either bank, and it is in that stretch that everything in this business actually happens.

The Section grades none of it. Not the tradecraft, not the planning, not what a man was carrying when he stepped off the boards. At first light a clerk in the customs hut writes down who is standing on which side of the white line, and that single sheet is the only thing that goes into the pouch.

Bill brought the wrong man over.

He had a flat above a locksmith on the eastern bank, two agents sitting in it, and one set of exit papers on the table between them. This is the third month running he has stood in a room with two men and chosen the one who could not walk. It has stopped looking like accident and started looking like method.

He signed out Kimani Vidal.

Vidal came across the bridge with 1.7 on him.

Sean Tucker stayed in the flat with 35.

That is a difference of 33.3, carried by the man who never left the eastern bank, and Tucker was not alone up there. By the time the barrier came down Bill had 47.1 stranded on the wrong side of the water, more than any man abandoned anywhere this week.

The clerk wrote his name on the correct side of the line.

Bill won by 17.92.

Coming the other way in the same darkness were Eric/Blakey, and they had done the hard thing properly. They had a defector. Josh Allen walked out of the east with 45.18 in his coat, 23.51 more than the man has ever been good for on an ordinary night, the sort of arrival that gets a station chief promoted and a debriefing room kept warm until morning.

They lost.

They went back to their own side of the canal at 3-8, ninth, holding the finest single piece of work anybody produced all night and a receipt for nothing.

Nobody at Gerberstrasse is credited for the walk. Only for the arrival.

Which brings me to Bryan, who runs the cleanest network in FantasyWorld and cannot get anyone home.

Understand what he does. Nothing is left in a drawer. No courier is asleep in a boarding house, no file is in a safe he forgot the combination to, no asset is sitting in a café waiting for a signal that never comes. His efficiency is 95.21 per cent, the best figure in this league, and on the night in question the sum total of what he failed to bring to the bridge was 4.2.

He put 98.62 on the boards.

Opposite him was Gabes, who left 34.9 locked in a drawer in another city entirely and did not appear to think about it once.

Gabes got there with 100.96.

2.34.

Nine men worked that river and eight of them beat Bryan. He is 4-7 and eighth. The one man he outscored was Bolek, and Bolek is the reason anyone still believes in mercy.

Bolek came to the middle of the bridge with 91.54 and a bag he never opened. There was 27.2 in it. Justin took him apart by 43.82 without breaking stride, went to 7-4 and second, and had the decency to look bored about it.

The belt is Bolek's for the third time. He has now held it two weeks running, which is what happens when a man is 0-9 against the field and still finds something to leave behind.

Upriver, Daniel had the night of his life and nobody came to meet him.

142.52. The highest anybody managed. He brought over everything he had and left 4.4 behind him, which is the closest thing to a clean extraction that exists out here, and the result of it is this: there was no man in FantasyWorld who could have beaten him. Nine out of nine.

The one he actually drew was Jack, who arrived on 112.24 holding first place in the league and went home third, beaten by 30.28 by a man who is 7-2 against him across their lives.

Daniel is seventh. Six wins, five defeats, a perfect night's work, and seventh.

Mario's radio man went silent halfway through and he won anyway. Justin Herbert managed 3.84 for him against an average of 22.18 — a whole channel down, dead air where the traffic should have been — and Mario still landed 135 and took Nate by 17.1. He is first in FantasyWorld and has scored 1594.74 this season, which is not a total any other man on this river is within reach of.

Nate had a hundred career wins waiting for him and did not get out of the water. Ninety-eight. He has been standing on ninety-eight for a fortnight now, two names short, and the last stretch of any bridge is the unlit one.

Four men left Gerberstrasse at 7-4 and the difference between first and fourth among them is not skill, it is who they happened to be walked out to meet.

At dawn the clerk came out of the hut, folded his sheet, and put it in the pouch. He did not ask Eric/Blakey what they had been carrying. He did not ask Bryan what he had not left behind. He does not record what a man brought, or what he was worth, or what it cost him to reach the paint.

Only which end of the bridge he came off.

Ten men in dinner jackets came up this week.

You may lay down the finest cards of your life on that baize and go back down the mountain with your pockets turned out, provided you have been seated across from the right person.

12.headline: Two flawless accounts presented at court, and only one man rises
12.issueTitle: Two Perfect Accounts and One Locked Drawer
12.deck: Justin and Bill each left nothing behind; the order of precedence rewarded one of them and shrugged at the other.
12.column:
The palace keeps one document that matters. It is copied out fresh each morning and nailed to the panelling outside the presence chamber: ten names, top to bottom, in order. Where your name sits is where you stand, who you walk out behind, and whether the sovereign's eye ever gets as far down the room as your face.

It is not amended by merit. It is amended by outcome.

Twice a year, if that, a man carries in his accounts and there is nothing whatever wrong with them. No coin left in a strongbox at his lodgings. No asset held back for a better morning. Sixty-five times in one thousand and ten presentations has anyone come to that table with their pockets genuinely turned out.

It happened twice before noon.

Justin laid down 137.68 and, when the clerk turned the page to look behind the total, there was nothing behind the total. He walked out of the chamber first in FantasyWorld, which is where he had been trying to get since August.

Bill did precisely the same thing.

Understand who this is. For three months Bill has come to this court with two men in his household and has walked the wrong one down the corridor, every single time, and has been waved through anyway. He has left better men shut in upstairs rooms in this palace and been advanced for it while they hammered on the doors.

This time he brought all of it. Every coin. 122.38, and the page behind it clean.

He lost by 19.14.

The man across the table from him was Gabes, who had come from apartments in which a drawer was locked. DJ Moore was in the drawer, worth 18.9. Gabes had instead brought Emeka Egbuka into the presence chamber and set him down in front of the clerk, and Egbuka was worth 3.7.

Nobody opens the drawer. That is the whole architecture of the place. The clerk records what is on the table and the chamberlain amends the sheet, and Gabes went up to third with seventeen and a half points of household goods sitting in the dark two streets away.

Bill did not move at all.

Now. Bryan.

For a season and a half this column has watched Bryan arrive with the tidiest books at court and leave without so much as a nod. He wastes less than any man here. He has spent the autumn being immaculate and being ignored, and there is no clause in the order of precedence that covers being right.

This time he arrived behind Jahmyr Gibbs.

51.9. Three times what the man is ordinarily good for, carried into the chamber in daylight, and behind it the largest sum anybody in the palace produced all morning.

153.12.

There was no courtier in FantasyWorld who could have stood against it. Nine out of nine.

The one actually set opposite him was Eric/Blakey, who came in with 90.64, the smallest offering in the building, and were beaten by 62.48 while every other man present would also have beaten them. There has been a case made in this column that their season is a matter of who they keep being paired with. Not this morning. This morning they were simply the poorest men in the room, and there were nine witnesses.

Bryan is 5-7. Eighth. He produced the finest morning's work at court and rose exactly nowhere, because the sheet does not backdate.

Which brings us to the wealthiest man in the palace.

Mario has 1720.04 this season. No one is close. Set him against the whole court, week upon week, and he beats it three times out of four. He arrived expecting the customary formalities.

Jonathan Taylor came in with 7.6 in his hands. He is a man who has averaged better than triple that all year, and he walked the length of the chamber and put down almost nothing, and the silence in that room was worth the price of admission.

Across the table stood Bolek, who is 3-9 and last in every column the palace keeps.

Mario lost by 8.

He had left 16.3 at home, which is what earns a man the black ribbon in this house, and the ribbon was tied on him without ceremony while he was still explaining. He came in first in FantasyWorld and left it fourth, three places lower, beaten by the poorest courtier present and wearing the badge of a man who did it to himself.

In the corridor outside all of this, Nate is still waiting.

There is a gallery here where the portraits hang, and a man's portrait goes up when he has a hundred victories against his name. Jack and Daniel were both hung in the autumn. Nate's frame has been standing against the corridor wall so long that the servants have stopped moving it to sweep behind.

Ninety-eight. Two more.

Jack, who put 145 on the table and took Nate apart by 32.72, has already been up there for weeks and had no particular use for the frame.

Justin, meanwhile, is on ninety-seven, and he has just taken the top of the sheet with a presentation nobody could fault.

Three men now stand at 8-4 and only the counting of coins separates them. Beneath them, holding more money than any of them, stands Mario in a black ribbon.

And Bill, fifth, exactly where he was, having finally done the thing the court claims to want.

The chamberlain nails up a fresh sheet in the morning. Bill's name will be in the same place it was, one line below a man who never came back for the drawer.

The bridge at Gerberstrasse is lit at both ends and dark in the middle. That is not an oversight. Two lamps, two barriers, and forty paces of nothing between them where a man cannot be seen from either bank, and it is in that stretch that everything in this business actually happens.

13.deck: Bolek leaves 30.7 buried in the ground, Bill brings in everything he owns and loses by 2.22, and two men come off the flats weighing the same to within 0.04.
13.column:
Kell has one working pump and it runs brown for the first minute.

The warden operates it on a rule nobody agreed to. Men go out into the dead country, come back dragging whatever they found, and at the gate they are set in pairs with their hauls on the beam. The heavier man drinks. The lighter man is walked back past the wire with a dry can. It does not matter how far he went, how clean he worked, or what it cost him to get home.

It matters who was standing at the other end of the scale.

Bryan has been coming to this gate for two seasons doing everything right and going back out thirsty.

His wire patrol had been worthless all year. Ten point two on an average trip, enough to justify the ammunition and nothing beyond that. This time it came over the ridge at dusk hauling a bowser on a rope and the packs of two men who were not with them any more.

32.5.

Behind it came the rest of it, and when the warden had finished loading the pan he had 158.36 on the beam, more than any man brought into Kell that week. There was no one on the plain who could have outweighed him. Nine out of nine.

The man they set opposite him was Bolek.

Across ten weighings in their lives Bolek has walked in heavier eight times. He is the one obstacle in this settlement that Bryan has never been able to shift. Bryan is 2-8 against him now, which is one better than it was, and the improvement was made by 47.36 of daylight.

Bolek came in with the lightest load at Kell.

What makes it worth writing down is what he did not come in with. Somewhere out on the flats there is a rock with a mark scratched on it that Bolek made himself, and under that rock is 30.7, and he walked past it on the way home. He is 3-10. Every man on the plain outweighed him. The yoke goes back around his neck, for the fourth time, which is more than anyone else in this place has had to wear it.

Now the part of the morning that a man should not look at directly.

Two survivors came off the salt at almost exactly the same weight. Nate had 113.3 in his pan. Gabes had 113.34.

0.04.

The difference between them is not measurable by any instrument at this station, and it decided nothing, because the beam does not compare all ten. Gabes was set against Justin, who came in at 111.86, and Gabes drank. He is 9-4 and second in FantasyWorld with a scavenging record that would embarrass a careful man.

Nate was set against Eric/Blakey, who came in at 126.96, and Nate was walked back out through the gate with an empty can for the third week running.

Same weight. Opposite ends of the yard. One of them heard the pump start.

There is a water tower over Kell with names cut into the steel of it, and a man's name is cut when he has survived a hundred weighings. Nate has ninety-eight strokes against him. He has had ninety-eight for a month. Justin has ninety-seven and went out dry as well, so the two of them are back on the flats together, walking in the same direction, neither able to get the last of it done.

Bill brought in everything he owned.

Understand what that means here. Most men bury something — a spare can, a coil of wire, a good man they could not carry. When the warden went through Bill's tracks he found 1.6 left behind in the whole of the dead country. Nothing. Twice now in three weeks he has come home stripped to the frame and correct, after three months of leaving the better half of his haul under a tarpaulin and being let through the gate regardless.

Jack outweighed him by 2.22.

Jack drank, and took first place in FantasyWorld at 9-4, and did not appear to notice how close it had been. Bill went back out at 6-7. Six men in Kell brought less than he did. All six of them were paired better.

Daniel did the opposite of Bill and was rewarded for it.

He left Terry McLaurin under a rock — 18.1, sitting in the shade, safe and useless — and carried Rome Odunze the whole way in on his shoulders for 1.3. That is what he chose to do with his strength. He then outweighed Mario by 12.12 and drank his fill.

Mario has hauled 1838.42 out of the wasteland this season, more than any man at this station by a distance nobody else can see the far side of, and he is 7-6. His best runner came back with 3.3 in an empty sack and no explanation.

Eric/Blakey found something at last, which after nine defeats is worth the ink, and went to the pump for the first time in a while.

The warden chalked the pairings for next week on the gatepost before the light went, the way he does, without looking up.

Bryan stood in the yard with the heaviest load anyone had brought to Kell all week, at 6-7, seventh in FantasyWorld, drinking water he should have been given a month ago.

Out past the wire, a rock with a mark on it. Under the rock, 30.7. It will be there in the morning.

priorColumns:
The bridge at Gerberstrasse is lit at both ends and dark in the middle. That is not an oversight. Two lamps, two barriers, and forty paces of nothing between them where a man cannot be seen from either bank, and it is in that stretch that everything in this business actually happens.

The Section grades none of it. Not the tradecraft, not the planning, not what a man was carrying when he stepped off the boards. At first light a clerk in the customs hut writes down who is standing on which side of the white line, and that single sheet is the only thing that goes into the pouch.

Bill brought the wrong man over.

He had a flat above a locksmith on the eastern bank, two agents sitting in it, and one set of exit papers on the table between them. This is the third month running he has stood in a room with two men and chosen the one who could not walk. It has stopped looking like accident and started looking like method.

He signed out Kimani Vidal.

Vidal came across the bridge with 1.7 on him.

Sean Tucker stayed in the flat with 35.

That is a difference of 33.3, carried by the man who never left the eastern bank, and Tucker was not alone up there. By the time the barrier came down Bill had 47.1 stranded on the wrong side of the water, more than any man abandoned anywhere this week.

The clerk wrote his name on the correct side of the line.

Bill won by 17.92.

Coming the other way in the same darkness were Eric/Blakey, and they had done the hard thing properly. They had a defector. Josh Allen walked out of the east with 45.18 in his coat, 23.51 more than the man has ever been good for on an ordinary night, the sort of arrival that gets a station chief promoted and a debriefing room kept warm until morning.

They lost.

They went back to their own side of the canal at 3-8, ninth, holding the finest single piece of work anybody produced all night and a receipt for nothing.

Nobody at Gerberstrasse is credited for the walk. Only for the arrival.

Which brings me to Bryan, who runs the cleanest network in FantasyWorld and cannot get anyone home.

Understand what he does. Nothing is left in a drawer. No courier is asleep in a boarding house, no file is in a safe he forgot the combination to, no asset is sitting in a café waiting for a signal that never comes. His efficiency is 95.21 per cent, the best figure in this league, and on the night in question the sum total of what he failed to bring to the bridge was 4.2.

He put 98.62 on the boards.

Opposite him was Gabes, who left 34.9 locked in a drawer in another city entirely and did not appear to think about it once.

Gabes got there with 100.96.

2.34.

Nine men worked that river and eight of them beat Bryan. He is 4-7 and eighth. The one man he outscored was Bolek, and Bolek is the reason anyone still believes in mercy.

Bolek came to the middle of the bridge with 91.54 and a bag he never opened. There was 27.2 in it. Justin took him apart by 43.82 without breaking stride, went to 7-4 and second, and had the decency to look bored about it.

The belt is Bolek's for the third time. He has now held it two weeks running, which is what happens when a man is 0-9 against the field and still finds something to leave behind.

Upriver, Daniel had the night of his life and nobody came to meet him.

142.52. The highest anybody managed. He brought over everything he had and left 4.4 behind him, which is the closest thing to a clean extraction that exists out here, and the result of it is this: there was no man in FantasyWorld who could have beaten him. Nine out of nine.

The one he actually drew was Jack, who arrived on 112.24 holding first place in the league and went home third, beaten by 30.28 by a man who is 7-2 against him across their lives.

Daniel is seventh. Six wins, five defeats, a perfect night's work, and seventh.

Mario's radio man went silent halfway through and he won anyway. Justin Herbert managed 3.84 for him against an average of 22.18 — a whole channel down, dead air where the traffic should have been — and Mario still landed 135 and took Nate by 17.1. He is first in FantasyWorld and has scored 1594.74 this season, which is not a total any other man on this river is within reach of.

Nate had a hundred career wins waiting for him and did not get out of the water. Ninety-eight. He has been standing on ninety-eight for a fortnight now, two names short, and the last stretch of any bridge is the unlit one.

Four men left Gerberstrasse at 7-4 and the difference between first and fourth among them is not skill, it is who they happened to be walked out to meet.

At dawn the clerk came out of the hut, folded his sheet, and put it in the pouch. He did not ask Eric/Blakey what they had been carrying. He did not ask Bryan what he had not left behind. He does not record what a man brought, or what he was worth, or what it cost him to reach the paint.

Only which end of the bridge he came off.

The palace keeps one document that matters. It is copied out fresh each morning and nailed to the panelling outside the presence chamber: ten names, top to bottom, in order. Where your name sits is where you stand, who you walk out behind, and whether the sovereign's eye ever gets as far down the room as your face.

It is not amended by merit. It is amended by outcome.

Twice a year, if that, a man carries in his accounts and there is nothing whatever wrong with them. No coin left in a strongbox at his lodgings. No asset held back for a better morning. Sixty-five times in one thousand and ten presentations has anyone come to that table with their pockets genuinely turned out.

It happened twice before noon.

Justin laid down 137.68 and, when the clerk turned the page to look behind the total, there was nothing behind the total. He walked out of the chamber first in FantasyWorld, which is where he had been trying to get since August.

Bill did precisely the same thing.

Understand who this is. For three months Bill has come to this court with two men in his household and has walked the wrong one down the corridor, every single time, and has been waved through anyway. He has left better men shut in upstairs rooms in this palace and been advanced for it while they hammered on the doors.

This time he brought all of it. Every coin. 122.38, and the page behind it clean.

He lost by 19.14.

The man across the table from him was Gabes, who had come from apartments in which a drawer was locked. DJ Moore was in the drawer, worth 18.9. Gabes had instead brought Emeka Egbuka into the presence chamber and set him down in front of the clerk, and Egbuka was worth 3.7.

Nobody opens the drawer. That is the whole architecture of the place. The clerk records what is on the table and the chamberlain amends the sheet, and Gabes went up to third with seventeen and a half points of household goods sitting in the dark two streets away.

Bill did not move at all.

Now. Bryan.

For a season and a half this column has watched Bryan arrive with the tidiest books at court and leave without so much as a nod. He wastes less than any man here. He has spent the autumn being immaculate and being ignored, and there is no clause in the order of precedence that covers being right.

This time he arrived behind Jahmyr Gibbs.

51.9. Three times what the man is ordinarily good for, carried into the chamber in daylight, and behind it the largest sum anybody in the palace produced all morning.

153.12.

There was no courtier in FantasyWorld who could have stood against it. Nine out of nine.

The one actually set opposite him was Eric/Blakey, who came in with 90.64, the smallest offering in the building, and were beaten by 62.48 while every other man present would also have beaten them. There has been a case made in this column that their season is a matter of who they keep being paired with. Not this morning. This morning they were simply the poorest men in the room, and there were nine witnesses.

Bryan is 5-7. Eighth. He produced the finest morning's work at court and rose exactly nowhere, because the sheet does not backdate.

Which brings us to the wealthiest man in the palace.

Mario has 1720.04 this season. No one is close. Set him against the whole court, week upon week, and he beats it three times out of four. He arrived expecting the customary formalities.

Jonathan Taylor came in with 7.6 in his hands. He is a man who has averaged better than triple that all year, and he walked the length of the chamber and put down almost nothing, and the silence in that room was worth the price of admission.

Across the table stood Bolek, who is 3-9 and last in every column the palace keeps.

Mario lost by 8.

He had left 16.3 at home, which is what earns a man the black ribbon in this house, and the ribbon was tied on him without ceremony while he was still explaining. He came in first in FantasyWorld and left it fourth, three places lower, beaten by the poorest courtier present and wearing the badge of a man who did it to himself.

In the corridor outside all of this, Nate is still waiting.

There is a gallery here where the portraits hang, and a man's portrait goes up when he has a hundred victories against his name. Jack and Daniel were both hung in the autumn. Nate's frame has been standing against the corridor wall so long that the servants have stopped moving it to sweep behind.

Ninety-eight. Two more.

Jack, who put 145 on the table and took Nate apart by 32.72, has already been up there for weeks and had no particular use for the frame.

Justin, meanwhile, is on ninety-seven, and he has just taken the top of the sheet with a presentation nobody could fault.

Three men now stand at 8-4 and only the counting of coins separates them. Beneath them, holding more money than any of them, stands Mario in a black ribbon.

And Bill, fifth, exactly where he was, having finally done the thing the court claims to want.

The chamberlain nails up a fresh sheet in the morning. Bill's name will be in the same place it was, one line below a man who never came back for the drawer.

14.headline: Daniel leaves 51.54 in the cages and is buckled into the belt
14.issueTitle: What Was Left Below the Sand
14.deck: Bill has the best morning anyone had and stays 7-7, while Bryan survives by 0.7 with a champion who gave him 0.4.
14.column:
The editor of the games does not fight, does not bleed and does not lose. He sits under the awning with a stick of chalk and sets the ten of them against each other, two names at a time, and that is the whole of his labour.

No man here chooses who he meets on the sand.

He chooses only which of his fighters come up out of the dark.

Beneath the arena there is a corridor of cages and a lift on four ropes, and a winchman who raises whoever he is pointed at and leaves the rest where they are.

Daniel went down there before the gates opened.

He walked the corridor with a lamp, past men who stood up when the light reached them, and he stopped and pointed at Jayden Daniels.

Two cages further along, Shedeur Sanders had both hands through the grille.

The lift went up. The bolt shot home behind it.

Daniels came out into the noise and gave Daniel 3.22.

Under the floor, in the dark, Sanders was worth 35.96. Between the two of them lay 32.74 points, one boy in the sunlight and one boy behind iron, and Daniel had personally decided which was which.

He was not finished. All along that corridor, when the sand was raked at the end of it, there was 51.54 left standing in cages.

What came up top was 98.76. Least of anyone in the building. Put him against every other man on the card and he loses to all nine of them, one after another, without a single reprieve.

The man the chalk had actually given him was Eric/Blakey, who have lost this pairing six times out of eight across their lives and who took him apart by 30.54 without ever appearing to hurry. Second win running. Still 5-9, still ninth, but they walked off the sand and Daniel did not.

Then the editor came down the steps himself, carrying the belt.

It is old bronze and it does not shine any more, because it is not given for defeat. Losing is ordinary here. The belt is for the man who arms the wrong half of his household and then goes out to die in front of a crowd. Bolek had worn it exactly one week. He handed it over without a word and Daniel stood there while it was buckled on him.

Justin's cages were empty.

All of them. The winchman went down after and had nothing to do; every door stood open, every man had been brought up into the light, and there was not one point left under that arena belonging to Justin.

He fought with the whole of what he owned and it came to 100.02.

Only one man in FantasyWorld did less. Against the field he goes 1-8. A morning of absolutely flawless preparation, and it was the second-smallest thing on the sand.

The man opposite him was Nate, who had 130.18 and rather a lot riding on it.

Because there is a wooden sword in this place. It hangs behind the editor's chair, and it is handed down to a fighter on his hundredth victory, at which point he is finished with the sand for good and everybody stands up.

Nate now has ninety-nine.

He has been walking toward that thing all autumn with the crowd getting quieter each week. He has it in his sight. He took the ninety-ninth off a man who did nothing wrong at all, which is how these things get taken.

Justin is on ninety-seven and went out through the far gate with a clean record and a beating.

Bryan's champion went down before the crowd had settled.

Jalen Hurts is worth better than twenty on an ordinary week. He fell in the opening moments, in front of everyone, and contributed 0.4 to the rest of the day.

Bryan won anyway.

By 0.7.

Understand what that is. For a season and a half this column has watched Bryan bring the tidiest, hardest, most complete work in FantasyWorld onto this sand and be sent home in the dark. He is now winning. He is winning with the seventh-best showing on the card, three men in the arena beat what he did and he still went to the gate. Third straight time.

The man he stepped over was Jack, who leads FantasyWorld at 9-5 and who, set against the whole card, goes 2-7.

Bill had the best morning anyone had.

147.52. Nine out of nine against the field. There was nobody in the building who could have stood in front of him, and the chalk had given him Bolek, who is 3-11 and who fought better than his season and lost by 30.1 for the trouble.

For three months Bill picked the wrong man out of the cages and was waved through regardless. Then he started bringing everything, and was beaten twice for it. This time he brought everything and it was rewarded, and at the end of it he is 7-7 and fifth, which is what this place pays for competence when the chalk is not in the mood.

Mario killed more than anyone again — 138.36, with 33.2 of it off Puka Nacua alone, and 1976.78 for the season, a number no other man in this arena can see the back of. It buys him third.

Gabes brought the fifth-best of the ten, which is more than he has brought in a month, and this was the week he was set against Mario. He lost 120.02 to it and stayed second.

When the crowd had gone, the winchman went back down with a lamp to open what was still locked.

He let Sanders out last. Thirty-five points and change came up the ramp into an arena with nobody in it, blinking at the light, ready.

priorColumns:
The palace keeps one document that matters. It is copied out fresh each morning and nailed to the panelling outside the presence chamber: ten names, top to bottom, in order. Where your name sits is where you stand, who you walk out behind, and whether the sovereign's eye ever gets as far down the room as your face.

It is not amended by merit. It is amended by outcome.

Twice a year, if that, a man carries in his accounts and there is nothing whatever wrong with them. No coin left in a strongbox at his lodgings. No asset held back for a better morning. Sixty-five times in one thousand and ten presentations has anyone come to that table with their pockets genuinely turned out.

It happened twice before noon.

Justin laid down 137.68 and, when the clerk turned the page to look behind the total, there was nothing behind the total. He walked out of the chamber first in FantasyWorld, which is where he had been trying to get since August.

Bill did precisely the same thing.

Understand who this is. For three months Bill has come to this court with two men in his household and has walked the wrong one down the corridor, every single time, and has been waved through anyway. He has left better men shut in upstairs rooms in this palace and been advanced for it while they hammered on the doors.

This time he brought all of it. Every coin. 122.38, and the page behind it clean.

He lost by 19.14.

The man across the table from him was Gabes, who had come from apartments in which a drawer was locked. DJ Moore was in the drawer, worth 18.9. Gabes had instead brought Emeka Egbuka into the presence chamber and set him down in front of the clerk, and Egbuka was worth 3.7.

Nobody opens the drawer. That is the whole architecture of the place. The clerk records what is on the table and the chamberlain amends the sheet, and Gabes went up to third with seventeen and a half points of household goods sitting in the dark two streets away.

Bill did not move at all.

Now. Bryan.

For a season and a half this column has watched Bryan arrive with the tidiest books at court and leave without so much as a nod. He wastes less than any man here. He has spent the autumn being immaculate and being ignored, and there is no clause in the order of precedence that covers being right.

This time he arrived behind Jahmyr Gibbs.

51.9. Three times what the man is ordinarily good for, carried into the chamber in daylight, and behind it the largest sum anybody in the palace produced all morning.

153.12.

There was no courtier in FantasyWorld who could have stood against it. Nine out of nine.

The one actually set opposite him was Eric/Blakey, who came in with 90.64, the smallest offering in the building, and were beaten by 62.48 while every other man present would also have beaten them. There has been a case made in this column that their season is a matter of who they keep being paired with. Not this morning. This morning they were simply the poorest men in the room, and there were nine witnesses.

Bryan is 5-7. Eighth. He produced the finest morning's work at court and rose exactly nowhere, because the sheet does not backdate.

Which brings us to the wealthiest man in the palace.

Mario has 1720.04 this season. No one is close. Set him against the whole court, week upon week, and he beats it three times out of four. He arrived expecting the customary formalities.

Jonathan Taylor came in with 7.6 in his hands. He is a man who has averaged better than triple that all year, and he walked the length of the chamber and put down almost nothing, and the silence in that room was worth the price of admission.

Across the table stood Bolek, who is 3-9 and last in every column the palace keeps.

Mario lost by 8.

He had left 16.3 at home, which is what earns a man the black ribbon in this house, and the ribbon was tied on him without ceremony while he was still explaining. He came in first in FantasyWorld and left it fourth, three places lower, beaten by the poorest courtier present and wearing the badge of a man who did it to himself.

In the corridor outside all of this, Nate is still waiting.

There is a gallery here where the portraits hang, and a man's portrait goes up when he has a hundred victories against his name. Jack and Daniel were both hung in the autumn. Nate's frame has been standing against the corridor wall so long that the servants have stopped moving it to sweep behind.

Ninety-eight. Two more.

Jack, who put 145 on the table and took Nate apart by 32.72, has already been up there for weeks and had no particular use for the frame.

Justin, meanwhile, is on ninety-seven, and he has just taken the top of the sheet with a presentation nobody could fault.

Three men now stand at 8-4 and only the counting of coins separates them. Beneath them, holding more money than any of them, stands Mario in a black ribbon.

And Bill, fifth, exactly where he was, having finally done the thing the court claims to want.

The chamberlain nails up a fresh sheet in the morning. Bill's name will be in the same place it was, one line below a man who never came back for the drawer.

Kell has one working pump and it runs brown for the first minute.

The warden operates it on a rule nobody agreed to. Men go out into the dead country, come back dragging whatever they found, and at the gate they are set in pairs with their hauls on the beam. The heavier man drinks. The lighter man is walked back past the wire with a dry can. It does not matter how far he went, how clean he worked, or what it cost him to get home.

It matters who was standing at the other end of the scale.

Bryan has been coming to this gate for two seasons doing everything right and going back out thirsty.

His wire patrol had been worthless all year. Ten point two on an average trip, enough to justify the ammunition and nothing beyond that. This time it came over the ridge at dusk hauling a bowser on a rope and the packs of two men who were not with them any more.

32.5.

Behind it came the rest of it, and when the warden had finished loading the pan he had 158.36 on the beam, more than any man brought into Kell that week. There was no one on the plain who could have outweighed him. Nine out of nine.

The man they set opposite him was Bolek.

Across ten weighings in their lives Bolek has walked in heavier eight times. He is the one obstacle in this settlement that Bryan has never been able to shift. Bryan is 2-8 against him now, which is one better than it was, and the improvement was made by 47.36 of daylight.

Bolek came in with the lightest load at Kell.

What makes it worth writing down is what he did not come in with. Somewhere out on the flats there is a rock with a mark scratched on it that Bolek made himself, and under that rock is 30.7, and he walked past it on the way home. He is 3-10. Every man on the plain outweighed him. The yoke goes back around his neck, for the fourth time, which is more than anyone else in this place has had to wear it.

Now the part of the morning that a man should not look at directly.

Two survivors came off the salt at almost exactly the same weight. Nate had 113.3 in his pan. Gabes had 113.34.

0.04.

The difference between them is not measurable by any instrument at this station, and it decided nothing, because the beam does not compare all ten. Gabes was set against Justin, who came in at 111.86, and Gabes drank. He is 9-4 and second in FantasyWorld with a scavenging record that would embarrass a careful man.

Nate was set against Eric/Blakey, who came in at 126.96, and Nate was walked back out through the gate with an empty can for the third week running.

Same weight. Opposite ends of the yard. One of them heard the pump start.

There is a water tower over Kell with names cut into the steel of it, and a man's name is cut when he has survived a hundred weighings. Nate has ninety-eight strokes against him. He has had ninety-eight for a month. Justin has ninety-seven and went out dry as well, so the two of them are back on the flats together, walking in the same direction, neither able to get the last of it done.

Bill brought in everything he owned.

Understand what that means here. Most men bury something — a spare can, a coil of wire, a good man they could not carry. When the warden went through Bill's tracks he found 1.6 left behind in the whole of the dead country. Nothing. Twice now in three weeks he has come home stripped to the frame and correct, after three months of leaving the better half of his haul under a tarpaulin and being let through the gate regardless.

Jack outweighed him by 2.22.

Jack drank, and took first place in FantasyWorld at 9-4, and did not appear to notice how close it had been. Bill went back out at 6-7. Six men in Kell brought less than he did. All six of them were paired better.

Daniel did the opposite of Bill and was rewarded for it.

He left Terry McLaurin under a rock — 18.1, sitting in the shade, safe and useless — and carried Rome Odunze the whole way in on his shoulders for 1.3. That is what he chose to do with his strength. He then outweighed Mario by 12.12 and drank his fill.

Mario has hauled 1838.42 out of the wasteland this season, more than any man at this station by a distance nobody else can see the far side of, and he is 7-6. His best runner came back with 3.3 in an empty sack and no explanation.

Eric/Blakey found something at last, which after nine defeats is worth the ink, and went to the pump for the first time in a while.

The warden chalked the pairings for next week on the gatepost before the light went, the way he does, without looking up.

Bryan stood in the yard with the heaviest load anyone had brought to Kell all week, at 6-7, seventh in FantasyWorld, drinking water he should have been given a month ago.

Out past the wire, a rock with a mark on it. Under the rock, 30.7. It will be there in the morning.

06.headline: Bryan sails a flawless ship and is boarded anyway
06.issueTitle: The Articles Contain No Clause For This
06.deck: Justin takes his fifth prize running, Bill's 163.2 buys him nothing, and two captains close on a hundred.
06.column:
Every ship in FantasyWorld carries the Articles nailed to the mainmast, and every man in the fleet has put his name to them.

They cover shares. They cover powder, and grog, and what is owed a man who loses a hand at the guns. They are very clear about who takes the prize.

They contain no clause whatsoever for a captain who does everything right.

Bryan sailed the cleanest ship anyone has seen this year.

Nothing loose on the deck. Every gun run out and manned, every hand awake, nobody snoring below where he could do no good. Whatever was aboard was above: 105.96 points, all of it working. It has happened 65 times in 1010 manager-weeks that a captain in this league came through a night with an empty hold. Bryan did it here, in a rising sea, alongside the fastest ship in the fleet.

Then the dark to windward changed shape.

Justin came down on him with 146.2 and took the ship in one pass. Not a chase. Not a fight. An errand.

Fifth prize in a row.

Bryan's crew went over the side in perfect order.

The best-kept ship in FantasyWorld is 2-4 and has lost three straight, and the Articles have nothing to say to him about it.

The heaviest hold in the fleet belonged to Bill. 163.2, more than any keel afloat this week, and 9-0 against the field, which is the plain statement that there was no ship on the water he would not have opened up.

The one that happened to be lying alongside him was Mario's, and Mario was no merchantman. 136.82, third-best haul of the night, guns still firing as she went down by the head.

Mario also went down with 24.02 still in the hold, and with his best topman good for nothing. Puka Nacua came out of the rigging with 3.8 in his hands. He averages 20.5. So Mario buckles on the belt at the capstan while his ship settles behind him, third loss running, and the fleet watches him do it.

Bill is 3-3.

That is what the fattest hold in FantasyWorld buys you out here.

Gabes left a man asleep.

Kendrick Bourne was in a hammock below the waterline with 18.2 points in him, and Emeka Egbuka was standing his watch on deck, where he produced 2.9. That is the whole story of the night and Gabes rigged it himself.

Daniel had spent fifteen years being beaten by this man — 2-7 against him, lifetime, a career of being outsailed by the same colours. He came out of the smoke anyway. Cam Skattebo went over the rail with 32.5 and the boarding did not take long.

Gabes lost by 20.66. He still has more points than anybody in the league and a 40-14 record against the field, which means he is the finest seaman here and has fallen to third in the only column that pays.

There is a harbour up the coast with a number painted on the seawall in white, six feet high, and two captains beating towards it.

Daniel's prize was the 99th of his career.

Jack's was the 98th.

Jack took Eric/Blakey by 12.24 with 111.12, which was the seventh-best day's work in a fleet of ten. He is 3-6 against the field and 5-1 in the standings. Some men hunt. Jack keeps finding the one ship in the sea slower than his own, and he has now found four in a row, and he is two from that wall.

Eric/Blakey have been under six times.

They posted the lowest score in FantasyWorld again, 98.88, beaten by every ship on the water. But here is the thing that will not leave them alone: they have taken 720.22 points out of this season, more than Bolek has, and Bolek has a win. Their guns work. They are simply always downwind of somebody, and there are no wins in the world for that.

Bolek went down to Nate, 128 to 105.58, and is 12-42 against the field — a hull that ships water in a flat calm.

So the fleet stands off the coast and counts what it has.

Justin has the weather gauge of the whole league. Bill has the treasure and the record of a man who has none. Gabes has every measure of quality and third place. Bryan has a ship without a single fault in her and three straight burials.

The Articles say the prize belongs to the ship that takes it.

They say nothing at all about the ship that deserved it.

Bryan has read his twice.

07.headline: Bryan outshoots the whole territory and loses by 1.46
07.issueTitle: No Bounty in This County for Marksmanship
07.deck: A career-best score, a perfect lineup and a fourth straight burial, while Gabes wins by leaving the wrong man behind a door
07.column:
The stage road runs west out of Chalk Wells and there is nothing on it for four days but grass, wind and the shale where the horses go lame.

The county posts no bounty for marksmanship. It pays for the man still standing when the dust settles. That is the entire law out here, and every man in FantasyWorld has had it read to him.

Bryan shot better this week than he has ever shot in his life.

He came up the street with the sun behind him and he did not waste a round. Everything he carried, he fired. Everything he fired, hit. When it was over there was not one cartridge left in his belt — not one, none, an empty loop where a spare should have been, because he had used the whole of what he owned.

164.56. The best day's shooting of his career, across seventy-six times he has stood in a street like this one.

It was also the second week running that he finished with nothing left over. A clean belt happens sixty-five times in a thousand and ten mornings out here. Bryan has now done it twice on the trot and been carried off both times.

Because Mario came up the other end of the street.

There was not a man in the territory Mario would have lost to that morning — nine of them out there, and he would have put every one of them in the dirt. He drew on the only one who had ever shot like this.

1.46.

That is the whole margin. That is what a life's best is worth in Chalk Wells.

They took Bryan's boots off in the street. Four in a row now, and 2-5, and there is still not a single mark against his shooting.

Mario walked into the land office with 990.40 taken out of this season, more than any man in the county, and signed his name to a 4-3.

Gabes rode out at first light with the wrong man in the saddle beside him.

A week ago he had left Kendrick Bourne asleep in the bunkhouse and paid for it. So this time he went in, woke Bourne, put him on a horse and took him along.

Bourne produced 1.9.

Behind the bunkhouse door, still asleep, Travis Hunter had 20.1 in him.

All told, Gabes left 33.6 in Chalk Wells. He has now made the same mistake in consecutive weeks with the same man at the centre of it, from opposite directions, which is no longer a bad morning. It is a habit.

He won by 23.74.

He won by 23.74 and climbed to second in the county, because the man he rode against was Nate, and Nate was the slowest thing on the plain. Every one of the nine other men would have beaten Nate this week. Every single one. He posted 106.26 and it goes down in the Ledger in red, and a man can go 0-9 against the field and still only lose the one fight that counts, which is the only mercy this country offers anybody.

Jack does not miss the slow ones.

He rode down Justin in open ground, 159.42 to 120.38, and Justin — who had not been beaten in five straight, who was sitting at the head of the table with the weather at his back — went down to third with dust in his teeth. Jack has taken five in a row now and sits 6-1.

Which brings us to the post.

At the county line there is a marker driven into the caliche, and burned into the wood is the figure 100. Two riders are standing at it.

Daniel has been at that post since last week. He needed one more crossing and he had Bill in front of him, and Bill has lost to Daniel most of the years they have both been alive, 3-6 across the whole of it.

Bill was waiting at the creek anyway, and he had Bo Nix with him.

Nix is a 17-a-day man. He put 40.96 on the ground.

Daniel went back down the road with 99 still on him. Bill took his third straight and is 4-3, and for once his powder went off in a fight that paid.

So Jack arrived at the marker in the same week, from the other direction, and stopped there too.

Two men. Same number. Neither past it.

And out beyond the last claim, in the part of the territory nobody rides to on purpose, Eric/Blakey buried the season's sixth body and then, at last, found somebody slower than they were.

Bolek came up the trail with 20.7 still packed in his saddlebags — food, water, ammunition, all of it strapped down and untouched while he starved in the open. He lost by 31.44. He is 1-6 and he wears the belt for it, and in fifty-four rides against the field he has come home ahead of thirteen.

Eric/Blakey are 1-6 as well. It took seven attempts and the weakest man in the county to get there, and they will take it, because out here a win is a win and nobody asks how you got it.

That is the point, and Bryan is the proof of it.

He fired everything he had. He hit everything he aimed at.

The county paid Mario.

08.issueTitle: What the Ground Kept at Hollow End
08.deck: The lightest load in FantasyWorld belonged to the best team in it, and twenty more never came up.
08.column:
The burial ground at Hollow End is opened one night a year, and the men of FantasyWorld open it themselves, with spades, with hooded lanterns, without speaking.

There are two rules at the gate.

You are weighed on what you carry out. Whatever stays in the ground stays in the ground, and by first light the holes have closed again from underneath.

Ten men went over the wall.

Gabes went in first, because Gabes has been the best of them at this all season.

He put his spade into the softest plot in the yard and James Cook came up out of it.

On an ordinary night Cook is worth 15.87. He came up out of Hollow End with 41.6 in him, and he came up alone.

Gabes worked the rest of the row and the rest of the row was thin. Bone dust. Split boxes. Things not worth the lifting.

He reached the gate at grey light with 95.26 across his shoulders and the sexton did not trouble with the scale, because there was not one man in the county who had not out-carried him.

Nought for nine.

The lightest load in FantasyWorld, taken out of the ground by the team that went in ranked ahead of everybody.

He had also left 20.52 down there. That is the third week running he has uncovered something with his own hands and walked away from it, and by the time he looked back the earth was already moving.

At the far wall, alone, digging badly, was Bolek.

Bolek is the worst of them at this and has been since the season opened: fourteen nights ahead of the field, fifty-eight behind.

He found 104.08 at Hollow End. That is nothing. That is a bad night in a bad year.

He carried out 104.08.

All of it. Not a rag, not a knuckle, not a coin left under the clay — one empty hole and one man walking down to the gate with everything the ground had offered him strapped to his back. Sixty-five times in 1010 nights has anybody come out of that yard clean.

The sexton weighed them both.

8.82.

Three years ago Gabes met this same man on this same night and out-carried him by 82.9.

He went into Hollow End first in FantasyWorld and came out of it fourth.

Bill had two lids in front of him and one crowbar.

Under the first was Rico Dowdle, who had come up out of the ground three times this autumn averaging 28.97, and who was, on all the evidence available at the graveside, the safest body in the yard.

Bill went to Dowdle. He got him open and found 6.4 in him.

The second lid he never touched. RJ Harvey was lying under it with 23.1.

Bill left 26.84 at Hollow End, more than any man in the league, and the ground had taken it before he was over the wall. At the gate the sexton had the belt waiting for him. Bolek unbuckled it and handed it across, having for once nothing whatsoever to answer for.

Nate opened only what he meant to open.

He carried 143.96 out of that yard and left an empty hole behind him, and he beat Bill by 28.56. Last time out every single man in the county dug more than Nate did. This time he went 6-3 against the field and stood at the gate with clean hands.

Set into the church wall at Hollow End there is a stone the sexton cuts, and two men in this league are one name short of a hundred.

Daniel came in needing it.

Bryan met him in the dark.

For four weeks Bryan has been the man the others carried out of this yard — the tidiest work in FantasyWorld, and a hole waiting for him at the end of every night. He climbed out of this one himself. 149.52, and 4.28 left behind, which is near enough to nothing.

Daniel went back down the road with ninety-nine still against his name. Bryan is 2-6 against him lifetime, and it took a hundredth win to make one of those two matter.

Jack came in needing it as well.

Mario was waiting at the top of the yard with 158.16 on his back, the heaviest load anyone took out of Hollow End this year, and 9-0 against the field, which is the plain statement that there was no man in the county he would have lost to.

Jack left 23.3 in the ground and went home on ninety-nine.

Two men. One number. The stone unchanged.

Justin took the second-heaviest load of the night, 152.02, left the yard almost bare and holds first place in FantasyWorld on 6-2. Eric/Blakey were beaten by 39.08 and are 1-7, and their only comfort is that they have taken more out of this season than Bolek has and will not be thanked for it.

By first light every hole in the yard had closed. Not been filled. Closed.

Bill's 26.84 was gone. So was the twenty Gabes had stood over and decided against, and whatever Jack had thought he could come back for.

The ground at Hollow End keeps what you leave in it.

It has never once cared who found it first.

The stage road runs west out of Chalk Wells and there is nothing on it for four days but grass, wind and the shale where the horses go lame.

The county posts no bounty for marksmanship. It pays for the man still standing when the dust settles. That is the entire law out here, and every man in FantasyWorld has had it read to him.

Bryan shot better this week than he has ever shot in his life.

He came up the street with the sun behind him and he did not waste a round. Everything he carried, he fired. Everything he fired, hit. When it was over there was not one cartridge left in his belt — not one, none, an empty loop where a spare should have been, because he had used the whole of what he owned.

It was also the second week running that he finished with nothing left over. A clean belt happens sixty-five times in a thousand and ten mornings out here. Bryan has now done it twice on the trot and been carried off both times.

Because Mario came up the other end of the street.

1.46.

Mario walked into the land office with 990.40 taken out of this season, more than any man in the county, and signed his name to a 4-3.

Gabes rode out at first light with the wrong man in the saddle beside him.

A week ago he had left Kendrick Bourne asleep in the bunkhouse and paid for it. So this time he went in, woke Bourne, put him on a horse and took him along.

At the county line there is a marker driven into the caliche, and burned into the wood is the figure 100. Two riders are standing at it.

Two men. Same number. Neither past it.

Eric/Blakey are 1-6 as well. It took seven attempts and the weakest man in the county to get there, and they will take it, because out here a win is a win and nobody asks how you got it.

That is the point, and Bryan is the proof of it.

He fired everything he had. He hit everything he aimed at.

The county paid Mario.

09.issueTitle: The Seating Plan at the Cassiopeia Club
09.deck: A flawless hand from Bryan is the worst in the room, and Anselm Vare's seating plan does the rest
09.column:
The Cassiopeia Club is cut into the top of a mountain and there is one way up to it, a cable car that leaves the valley station when the man in the booth decides it should.

Ten men in dinner jackets came up this week.

The house rule is printed nowhere and everybody knows it. The Cassiopeia does not pay the best hand in the room. It pays the man whose opponent did worse. You may lay down the finest cards of your life on that baize and go back down the mountain with your pockets turned out, provided you have been seated across from the right person.

Anselm Vare does not gamble. Vare does the placards.

Before the car arrives he walks the five tables with a leather folder under his arm, setting the little printed names down on the cloth, and then he stands at the window with a drink he never finishes and watches the weather come over the ridge. That is the entire scheme. Nobody has worked out how to beat it because there is nothing to beat. He decides who is opposite whom, and the mountain does the rest.

On the gallery above the floor there is a private room with a brass hundred screwed to the door.

Daniel had been standing outside it for three weeks.

Twice he had gone to the table needing one win and twice he had come back up the stairs and found the handle would not turn. This time Vare seated him across from Bolek, and dealt him a man nobody in the room had ever looked at twice.

Brock Bowers has been worth 3.94 a night all season. He fetches drinks. He stands behind chairs.

He sat down and put 35.3 on the cloth.

Bolek did not fold. He went to 119.28, which for Bolek is a genuine night's work, the best hand he has laid down in weeks, and it was short.

3.48.

The door on the gallery opened. Daniel went through it with one hundred career wins behind him, which is fifteen seasons of climbing this mountain, and the room did not stop for him because the room never stops for anybody.

Jack had come up the cable car on ninety-nine as well.

Vare had put him opposite Gabes, and Gabes arrived with his coat empty.

That is worth saying plainly. For three straight weeks Gabes has left money in his pockets — a man asleep in a bunkhouse, twenty points behind a locked door, a good hand held back for no reason anybody could name. This week he put down 148.54 and kept 1.5. Nothing hidden, nothing saved, nothing to answer for.

Jack managed 108.44. Eight of the nine other men in the room beat it. He went back down in the cable car with ninety-nine still against his name and two losses on the trot, and the brass door stayed shut.

Nate is on ninety-seven and climbing, three short, and he got there by doing something the house has always been happy to arrange.

He was seated across from Bryan.

Bryan played a flawless hand. Every card he was holding, he played. When the dealer cleared the table there was nothing left in his fingers — not one point on the bench, the second time in a handful of weeks he has emptied his hand completely, and it is the rarest thing anyone does at the Cassiopeia.

101.06.

The worst hand in the room. Every man on that mountain beat it. Nine out of nine, and the one sitting opposite him was Nate, who has now taken seven of the eight nights the two of them have ever spent at the same table.

Beaten by 42.04. Third in the league for efficiency all year, first actually, and 3-6, and back down the mountain in the dark.

Bill had the biggest stack of the night.

165.12, and there was not a man in the Cassiopeia he would have lost to. Vare sat him opposite Justin, who came up here holding first place, and Bill took 35.06 off him without hurrying.

And Justin walked out still top of the table, 6-3, because three men now hold that record and he has taken more off this season than either of them.

The house pays who the house pays.

Which brings us to the man who has taken more money out of this season than anybody alive and cannot get down the mountain with it.

Mario has 1294.44 for the year. Nobody is close. He sat down against Eric/Blakey, who have won twice in nine attempts, and he left 25.7 in his coat pocket — Alec Pierce with 16 in him, folded in the lining, in favour of Deebo Samuel and 4.9 on the cloth.

Eric/Blakey put down 161.18 and took the night by 15.3. Eight of the nine men in the room would have lost to them, which is the first time all season the seating plan has done them a kindness rather than an injury.

Mario is 5-4. At the cloakroom they handed him the belt.

By the time the last car went down, the gallery door had closed again with Daniel inside it, and the floor was being swept, and Vare was at the window with the folder open on the sill, laying out next week's placards in the dark.

He never looks at anyone's cards.

He only needs to know who is sitting opposite them.
